title: Rehat at work
hook: keeping the articles of faith in workplaces far from Punjab

segments.voice: Yesterday, children and rehat: amrit waits for understanding, and the child grows up inside the practice. Your line was when they understand. Did you check that someone understood what you asked? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

Five forty-five in the morning, a hospital locker room. A nurse finishes Japji on her phone with one earbud in, ties her hair under a surgical cap, slides her kara up her forearm and tapes it for the shift. Across town a cook pulls a net over his beard before the first ticket prints. On a building site, a foreman raises, once again, the question of a hard hat over his turban. None of them are in Punjab. All of them are keeping a code written for a whole people, among coworkers who may never have read it. Last week we looked at the kirpan and the law. Today is smaller and more daily: an ordinary shift, with the rehat along for it.
screen: `A NURSE, A COOK, A FOREMAN.` → `FAR FROM PUNJAB.` → `AN ORDINARY SHIFT, WITH THE REHAT ALONG.`

segments.voice: Start with the job itself. In Sikh teaching, it is part of the path. Guru Nanak puts it in one line on Ang 1245, in paraphrase: the one who eats what they earn by their own effort, and gives some of it away, has recognized the way. Earning honestly has a name, kirat. In that line it isn't a break from the spiritual life; earning sits right beside giving. So a Sikh at work isn't stepping out of the rehat for the length of a shift. The workplace is one more place it gets kept. Then the practical side. The articles of faith go to work too. The kesh stays uncut and covered, under a turban, a patka, a cap, a net. The kara stays on the wrist. The kirpan is worn in whatever way the place and its laws allow. That often takes conversations: with a manager, a safety officer, a uniform supplier. Sikhs in different countries have had those conversations, one workplace at a time, and the answers vary from place to place. And there's a third side, the one that belongs to everyone else. A colleague's turban, beard or kara is not a costume or a quirk. It's a promise, kept on company time. Respect at work can be as simple as asking a real question, once, and then letting it be normal. So rehat at work turns out to be three things at once. The work itself is honest earning, part of the path. The articles go along, worked out shift by shift. And the people around them get a small chance to make room.
screen: `ANG 1245: EARN, AND GIVE SOME AWAY.` · `KIRAT: HONEST WORK IS PART OF THE PATH.` · `THE ARTICLES GO TO WORK TOO.` · then, large: `A PROMISE, KEPT ON COMPANY TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a colleague's practice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you work or study with whose faith, or diet, or prayer times, or clothing differs from yours. Picture them for a moment going through their day, quietly keeping something that matters to them. Notice whether you've ever made that harder, even by a joke or a sigh. Then picture one small way to make it easier: a meeting time, a lunch order, a plain question asked kindly. The bell holds the time.
Rehat at work. For Sikhs, honest work is part of the path, and the articles of faith go to the job too, worked out with each workplace. Today's word.
Your line: faith at work. Today, at work or at school, notice one thing someone keeps for their faith, and make one small bit of room for it. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the articles of faith wear them at work, adapting to safety rules and uniforms (a patka or net over the kesh, a kara taped for a shift), and Sikh teaching counts honest earning, kirat, as part of the path.
